analysis.one_liner: Taxes chemical discharges, farm chemicals, and industrial water use to fund clean water projects and affordable water bills.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a floor vote: after one hearing in March 1994, it sat in three House committees until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have more than doubled federal clean water spending to $6 billion a year, paid for by new taxes on chemical discharges, fertilizers, pesticides, and nonresidential water use instead of general taxpayers. It would have expanded low-cost loans and grants to small towns and hard-pressed communities, and created a program capping water and sewer bills for low-income households at roughly 4% of their income. It was referred to three House committees, got a single hearing, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Small towns of 5,000 or fewer people and communities where water and sewer bills exceed 2% of median family income would become eligible for grant help rather than loans alone. Low-income households — including renters who pay water as part of rent — would get an assurance program designed to keep combined water and sewer bills at or below about 4% of gross monthly income for households earning up to 150% of the poverty line. States would have to spend at least 15% of their federal water money on polluted runoff control, and could fund wetlands restoration, watershed planning, and water conservation. The EPA had estimated more than $155 billion in clean water needs over 20 years, against about $2 billion a year in federal support at the time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small towns and low-income water customers

how_it_helps.text: Triples federal clean water investment to $6 billion a year — $2 billion from the general fund plus $4 billion from a new Clean Water Trust Fund — against an EPA-estimated need of over $155 billion over 20 years.

Makes small communities of 5,000 people or fewer and 'hardship' communities where average water and sewer bills reach 2% of median family income eligible for outright grants from state revolving funds, not just loans they must repay.

Creates a low-income water and sewer assurance program requiring that water and sewer service be affordable — presumptively no more than 4% of gross monthly income — for households at or below 150% of the federal poverty level, with benefits explicitly covering tenants who pay water through their rent.

Requires states to spend at least 15% of each federal capitalization grant on controlling nonpoint source pollution (polluted runoff), and expands eligible projects to wetlands protection and restoration, watershed management, coastal nonpoint programs, and public water conservation.

Pays for it under a polluter-pays structure: per-pound excise taxes on discharges of hundreds of listed chemical pollutants (from 0.6 cents to $63.39 per pound for the worst group, including mercury, PCBs, and dioxin), taxes on fertilizer, pesticides, and animal feed, and 1.95 cents per thousand gallons on nonresidential water use — while exempting residential households, farms, and government from the discharge and water-use taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and industrial dischargers would pay per-pound taxes on hundreds of listed pollutants. Fertilizer, pesticide, and animal feed manufacturers would pay new excise taxes, which would likely be passed along to farmers and eventually to food prices. Commercial and industrial water users would pay 1.95 cents per thousand gallons, collected through their water utilities. Residential households, farms, and government users are explicitly exempted from the discharge and water-use taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers, farm-chemical producers, industrial water users

drawbacks.text: The fertilizer, pesticide, and animal feed taxes are levied on manufacturers, who would likely pass them through to farmers as higher input costs and on to consumers as food prices.
The 1.95-cent-per-thousand-gallon tax on nonresidential water use would raise operating costs for businesses that use large volumes of water, some of which would be passed to customers.

The bill's own findings call the $4 billion in polluter taxes a contribution to 'deficit reduction and pollution control,' but the text dedicates the new tax revenue entirely to a trust fund for clean water spending, so it would not actually reduce the deficit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: $6 billion a year for water infrastructure, grant relief for small and financially strapped towns, and an affordability guarantee for low-income households facing rising water bills. The costs fall mainly on industries the bill identifies as contributors to water pollution — chemical dischargers and farm-chemical makers — with some pass-through to farmers and consumers. The main honest concerns are the pass-through of the agricultural input taxes into food prices and the fact that the 'deficit reduction' framing in the findings does not match the bill's actual spending of the new revenue. On balance the design matches its stated polluter-pays principle, though its heavy tax list would have drawn serious opposition in the tax-writing committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, got one hearing in March 1994, and was never approved by any committee or voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerry Studds of Massachusetts introduced the bill on May 20, 1993 with six original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Public Works and Transportation, and Ways and Means Committees.
Within a week it went to subcommittees in two of those committees, and the House requested the EPA's views; no committee ever took further formal action on the bill itself.
On March 3, 1994 the record cross-references H.R. 3948, a separate clean water bill, and on March 15, 1994 a committee hearing was held; that hearing was the bill's last recorded action.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill still stuck in committee, never reported out and never voted on by the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and fertilizer, pesticide, and feed makers never faced the new excise taxes, and taxpayers were never asked to fund the additional $4 billion a year; meanwhile small towns and low-income households got no relief from rising water and sewer bills, and the cross-referenced clean water reauthorization vehicle (H.R. 3948) also failed to become law.

for.name: Gerry Studds
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MA); Chairman, House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on it twice, and his committee held the bill's only hearing.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Tax-writing committee with jurisdiction over the bill's excise tax title
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never reported the bill or acted on its tax provisions.

against.name: House Public Works and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over water infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and referred it to a subcommittee; never reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no vote split exists; its 16 cosponsors were 15 Democrats and 1 Republican, and no recorded opposition appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would tax every pound of hundreds of listed chemical pollutants discharged to water or treatment plants, at rates up to $63.39 per pound for the most toxic group (mercury, PCBs, dioxin, DDT). The industry's interest in killing the bill ran directly against the public's interest in cleaner water funded by polluters.

industries.industry: Fertilizer, pesticide, and animal feed manufacturers
industries.note: New excise taxes of 0.845 cents per pound of fertilizer nutrients, 24.27 cents per pound of pesticide active ingredient, and $2.68 per ton of feed, applied at manufacture or import. Costs would likely pass through to farmers and food prices, but the tax targets products the bill identifies as contributing to water pollution.
A 1.95-cent tax per thousand gallons on nonresidential water use, collected by utilities, with residential, farm, hydroelectric, and government uses exempt.

industries.industry: Municipal water and sewer utilities and local governments
industries.note: The bill expands state revolving fund eligibility, allows grants to small and hardship communities, and triples the federal investment behind sewage treatment and runoff control projects these utilities build.

Farms are exempt from the chemical discharge tax and the water-use tax, but the fertilizer, pesticide, and feed taxes would raise input costs; in return, farmers would benefit from runoff-control funding under the expanded program.
